stories.headline: Update: Trump Calls Off Iran Strikes, Contingent on 'Rapid' Nuclear Deal
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump announced Sunday he is canceling a planned military strike on Iran, contingent on the two sides reaching a deal "rapidly," including a resolution to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to all shipping. Trump touted progress in diplomatic talks and pointed to Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's push for de-escalation as a contributing factor. No strikes were reported from either side overnight following the announcement.

Iranian state media struck a defiant tone in response, with outlets mocking Trump with headlines such as "Trump the fool has run out of steam" and asserting that Tehran had not asked for the attacks to be called off. Iranian news agencies gave no indication that the country's position on the Strait of Hormuz had changed. Iran has repeatedly sought to control maritime traffic through the waterway, which carried roughly one-fifth of the world's oil supply before the conflict escalated.

The diplomatic opening comes as the State Department issued a travel warning urging Americans in the Middle East to "consider departing now" and cautioning travelers to prepare for flight cancellations and airspace closures. Trump simultaneously signaled renewed pressure on Israel to halt strikes in Gaza, as Palestinian civilian casualties continued despite his announcement of a breakthrough several days prior.

The situation remains highly fluid. Supporters of the administration's approach argue that Trump's combination of military pressure and diplomacy has brought Iran to the table, while critics contend the pattern of threatened strikes followed by withdrawals has undermined U.S. credibility and emboldened Tehran's public posture.

stories.headline: Update: Spain's Sánchez Demands Emergency EU Ministers Meeting After Ceuta Migrant Surge
stories.summary:
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called for an emergency meeting of all 27 European Union interior ministers on Sunday, escalating a diplomatic dispute that erupted after tens of thousands of migrants crossed from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. In a letter addressed to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and other EU leaders, Sánchez sharply criticized fellow member states for what he called "selfish, polarising and unlawful" responses to the crisis.

Sánchez specifically appeared to target Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, whose government temporarily suspended Schengen Area free-travel arrangements with Spain in the wake of the surge. He argued the suspension was contrary to European law and humanitarian principles, noting that Spain had already expelled nearly all of the estimated 50,000–60,000 migrants back to Morocco and pointing out that Ceuta is not part of the Schengen Area.

The standoff has exposed deep fault lines within the EU over immigration enforcement, border sovereignty, and the limits of European solidarity. Meloni and other right-leaning European governments have framed the incident as a failure of Spanish border control and a test of the Schengen system's integrity, while Sánchez and allies argue Spain acted swiftly and that punishing Madrid sets a damaging precedent.

The crisis is the latest flash point in Europe's long-running debate over migration policy and comes as several member states have moved to reassert national border controls in recent years. The outcome of any emergency EU meeting could have significant implications for the future of the Schengen Area and the bloc's collective approach to external border management.

stories.headline: Iranian-Linked Crime Network Recruits Teenage Hitmen Across Europe, Europol Warns
stories.summary:
A Europol-backed investigative task force has documented a systematic pattern in which an Iranian-linked organized crime network known as the Foxtrot Network has recruited teenagers across Europe to carry out murders and attacks for cash, often through social media in a "gamified" format designed to mimic video games. The network is believed responsible for approximately 35 murders since 2022, as well as explosive and grenade attacks on Israeli targets in multiple countries.

The Foxtrot Network is led by Rawa Majid, a Swedish-based criminal who fled to Tehran after coming under investigation. According to Swedish investigative journalist Diamant Salihu, Majid struck a deal with the Iranian regime to carry out attacks against dissidents, journalists, and Israeli targets in exchange for protection. Law enforcement officials say the network deliberately recruits vulnerable teenagers who are often caught before any payment is made.

A Norwegian teenager, Johannes Natland, was convicted Wednesday at London's Old Bailey of conspiracy to murder for a planned killing in West Yorkshire — the latest in a series of arrests across 11 countries now involved in Europol's Operational Taskforce GRIMM, which spans Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Iceland, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain, Sweden, and the United Kingdom. The UK government sanctioned Majid and the Foxtrot Network in April 2025.

Andy Kraag, head of Europol's European Serious and Organised Crime Centre, described the phenomenon as the "calculated outsourcing of murder" to young people. The disclosures raise significant concerns about the reach of state-linked criminal networks inside Europe and the vulnerability of minors to online recruitment by foreign-backed criminal enterprises.

stories.headline: Update: DR Congo Ebola Death Toll Passes 1,500 as Uganda Contains Outbreak With Only Two Deaths
stories.summary:
The Ebola outbreak in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo has surpassed 1,500 confirmed deaths, making it the second-worst on record, with Congolese authorities warning Thursday that the virus is spreading faster than in any previous outbreak. Experts believe the true fatality count is substantially higher than official figures, and the World Health Organization has described the situation as deeply alarming.

In stark contrast, neighboring Uganda — which also recorded its first imported cases in May — has effectively contained the disease, releasing its last patient from hospital two weeks ago with only 20 confirmed cases and two deaths. WHO Uganda chief Dr. Kasonde Mwinga attributed the outcome not to luck but to decades of deliberate investment in epidemic preparedness, including rapid deployment of a specialist Ebola treatment center that had been kept in a state of readiness from a previous outbreak.

Public health officials point to Uganda's experience managing nine prior Ebola outbreaks since 2000 as the key differentiator. Ugandan authorities activated isolation protocols immediately upon confirming the first imported case, and subsequent patients sought treatment directly at the designated facility rather than passing through the community, limiting transmission chains. Of Uganda's 20 confirmed cases, 15 were individuals who had crossed from DR Congo.

The divergent outcomes illustrate the critical role of institutional preparedness and public trust in containing hemorrhagic fever outbreaks. Global health experts say the lessons from Uganda's response — including rapid facility activation, community communication, and cross-border coordination — could be applicable to future outbreak responses in the region.

stories.headline: Three Killed, Several Wounded in Shooting at Idaho In-N-Out Burger
stories.summary:
A gunman opened fire at an In-N-Out Burger restaurant in Twin Falls, Idaho, on Saturday afternoon, killing three people and wounding seven others, some critically, according to city officials. Police who responded to what a spokesperson described as a 'very chaotic scene' near a busy shopping area found the suspected gunman dead in an area near the restaurant. Twin Falls city public information officer Josh Palmer confirmed the fatalities but did not immediately provide details on whether the suspect died from self-inflicted wounds or a police encounter.

Law enforcement from multiple agencies responded to the scene. Authorities have not publicly identified the suspect or released a motive as of Saturday evening. The shooting drew immediate national attention given its location at a popular fast-food chain in a mid-sized Idaho city.

The incident is the latest in a series of mass shooting events at public commercial locations in the United States. Twin Falls has a population of roughly 50,000 and is the largest city in southern Idaho. No additional suspects were reported to be at large.

stories.headline: Indonesia Ferry Fire Kills Five, Leaves 41 Missing with Over 250 Aboard
stories.summary:
A passenger ferry carrying at least 250 people caught fire off Madura island in Indonesia on Saturday, killing five people and leaving 41 missing, according to Basarnas, the country's National Search and Rescue Agency. The vessel, KMP Mutiara Sentosa 2, was sailing from Surabaya in East Java to Makassar in South Sulawesi when the fire broke out between 6:00 and 7:00 a.m. local time.

Footage broadcast by Indonesian news outlets showed large numbers of passengers in life jackets crowding lifeboats and the ship's bow and bridge while awaiting rescue, with flames and heavy smoke visible from the upper decks. Rescue personnel were seen throwing lifebuoys to passengers who had jumped into the sea. Basarnas confirmed the ferry was 'almost entirely engulfed in flames' by the time rescuers arrived.

The cause of the fire had not been determined as of Saturday. The missing persons count raised concerns that the death toll could rise significantly. Indonesian maritime disasters involving ferries are not uncommon in the archipelago nation, which relies heavily on sea transport across its thousands of islands.

stories.headline: Zelensky Asks Trump to Press Musk on Expanding Starlink Access for Ukrainian Drone Strikes
stories.summary:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky asked President Donald Trump during a closed-door Oval Office meeting to persuade Elon Musk to allow Ukraine to use Starlink satellite connectivity to support drone strikes against Russia, according to multiple reports. The meeting took place during Zelensky's trip to the United States to attend the memorial service for Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.).

Starlink, operated by Musk's SpaceX, has been a critical communications infrastructure for Ukraine throughout the war with Russia. Musk has previously placed restrictions on how Ukraine can use the service, including blocking its use in certain offensive operations near Crimea in 2023. The latest request signals Kyiv's continued effort to expand the operational scope of Starlink-enabled drone warfare.

The request places Trump in a potentially awkward position, as he has maintained a complex relationship with both Zelensky and Musk. The White House has not publicly commented on what, if any, commitments Trump made during the meeting. The development comes amid ongoing fighting in Ukraine and continued diplomatic efforts to broker a ceasefire.

stories.headline: Update: Italy Places Nearly All Major Cities on Highest Heat Alert as European Wildfires Continue
stories.summary:
Italy's health ministry placed 19 major cities, including Rome, Milan, Venice, and Naples, on red alert Saturday as a new heatwave driven by a North African subtropical anticyclone intensified across the country. By Monday, 25 of Italy's 27 major cities are expected to be at the highest alert level, with temperatures reaching the mid-30s Celsius and authorities warning of dangers even to healthy adults. Residents were urged to stay indoors between 11 a.m. and 6 p.m. and remain hydrated.

The Italian alerts come as wildfires continued to burn across southern Europe. In France, roughly 2,500 people were evacuated in the Var region after a previously contained blaze reignited, though a major Gironde fire was brought under control and 200,000 evacuated residents were allowed to return home. In Greece, hundreds of tourists were evacuated by sea from a coastal town, while Spain has seen more than 200,000 hectares burn in 2026 — roughly five times above the seasonal average.

Scientists attribute the intensifying pattern to climate change, noting that Europe is warming twice as fast as the global average according to the Copernicus Climate Change Service. The successive heatwaves have created increasingly favorable conditions for wildfires across the Mediterranean basin. This story is a fresh development from previously covered European wildfire and heatwave coverage, with Italy's nationwide red alert system activation representing a new escalation.
